verdict: OK to lend in Faridabad engineering & capital goods — pursue asset-backed OEM/auto-component and export-linked fabricators with order visibility; avoid pure EPC and thin-margin wind/transmission players until margins stabilise.
title: Faridabad Engineering & Capital Goods: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
**Faridabad engineering runs on metal in, machined parts out, and cash back through receivables.** A unit buys steel and castings, converts them on CNC and press lines, and sells to auto OEMs, railways, power T&D and export buyers. Cash sits in inventory (raw plus WIP) and in receivables from large buyers; the working-capital cycle is the whole game, and CRISIL notes EPC players carry a longer cash conversion cycle than OEMs [11]. So when a proposal lands, check the receivable days against the buyer mix; if one OEM is over half of sales, ask for the purchase-order and payment terms in writing.

## What has changed now
**The national demand signal is strong: IIP for NIC 28 output is +10.3% YoY and +10.4% Apr-to-date [D], and exports are +19.8% Apr-to-date in USD [D].** Haryana GST collections are running +10.1% Apr-to-date versus India +6.1% [D], a genuine local tailwind. But peers show margin strain even on growth: Suzlon grew revenue 26% to Rs 4,869 crore while EBITDA margin narrowed to 14.8% from 18.6% [7], and Pitti is expanding amid margin strain [4]. **Growth is real; pricing power is not automatic.** So when a proposal shows rising sales with flat EBITDA, ask for the price-escalation clause with the buyer.

## Where the growth is
**Pursue auto-component and precision-machining suppliers to OEMs, export-linked fabricators, and firms feeding power T&D and data-centre demand.** Skipper posted its highest-ever Q2 revenue with PAT up 56% and strong export growth [6]; DEE's order book crossed Rs 1,300 crore with revenue up 77% to Rs 286.7 crore [5]; Pitti cites AI data-centre and global sourcing demand as structural [4]. Talbros is expanding in Faridabad itself [1]. **Avoid pure-play EPC and thin-margin wind/transmission subcontractors** until their margins recover.

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the working-capital cycle, not the P&L.** Take monthly stock-and-receivable statements, sanction limits against a defined drawing power, and insist on hypothecation of current assets plus a second charge on the Faridabad property. Note that Faridabad is also an NPA and loan-settlement hub [2] — so check the promoter's prior settlement history before sanction; if any settled account appears, ask for the OTS letter and closure proof. Collect from customer: current order book value, buyer-wise receivable ageing, and EBITDA margin trend.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch receivable days, inventory days and buyer concentration monthly.** If receivable days stretch beyond the sanctioned cycle for two months, cut drawing power and ask for the buyer's payment confirmation. If EBITDA margin falls while sales rise, reprice or reduce exposure. If a single buyer crosses half of sales, seek a second-buyer order before enhancing limits.
watch: Receivable days stretch two months running -> cut drawing power, seek buyer payment confirmation
Margin falls while sales rise -> reprice or trim exposure
One buyer crosses half of sales -> require second-buyer order before limit enhancement
Promoter CIBIL and settlement history (at sanction and annually)
Any prior OTS or settled account -> obtain OTS letter and closure proof before sanction
Order book and export order position (quarterly)
Order book falls or export orders stall -> freeze fresh capex-linked limits
